name: SIA Project 25 26
description:
In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: [https://iris.sad.ve.it/](https://iris.sad.ve.it/?utm_source=gemini). The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source software to all Italian public administrations through the portal [https://developers.italia.it/](https://developers.italia.it/?utm_source=gemini).

A. REPORTS
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin (which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its file path on the server). The possible problem categories are:
• Waterworks – Drinking water
• Architectural Barriers
• Sewerage
• Public Lighting
• Waste
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights
• Roads and Urban Furniture
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds
• Other
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), two cases are possible:

* Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer can mark the report as resolved.
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company (bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if previously configured by the municipal administrator.
* Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state.

C. CITIZEN UPDATES
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo).
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the same rules as for their own reports).

D. STATISTICS
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.

To have the option to submit reports without their name being publicly displayed.

branch_001.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Citizens to Report Urban Issues
branch_001.rationale: The initial goals (registration, account activation, and profile setup) are foundational steps that establish a citizen's identity and presence within the system. These steps are necessary prerequisites for the subsequent, core functionality of submitting detailed reports about urban issues, which include textual descriptions, multimedia attachments, geographical location, and categorization. All these operations collectively serve the purpose of empowering citizens to effectively communicate and report problems in their urban environment.

branch_002.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Citizens to Monitor and Manage Their Submitted Reports
branch_002.rationale: The low-level goals collectively aim to provide citizens with comprehensive tools to track the status and history of their submitted reports, receive timely updates, and control their notification preferences. This ensures citizens are well-informed and have agency over their interactions with the reporting system.

branch_003.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the functionalities required for a citizen to engage in a two-way communication with a municipal operator concerning a specific report, including the ability to send messages, receive responses, and review the entire conversation history. This ensures transparency and effective resolution of reports through direct dialogue.

branch_004.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable citizens to submit anonymous reports
branch_004.rationale: Both low-level goals directly contribute to the overarching objective of providing and maintaining anonymity for citizens when they submit reports. One goal focuses on the user's ability to choose anonymity, and the other focuses on the system's responsibility to enforce it.

branch_005.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Citizen monitors public reports submitted by other citizens.
branch_005.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe how a citizen can discover, organize, and stay informed about public reports submitted by other citizens, which are all facets of monitoring these reports.

branch_006.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Non-Registered Users to Access and View Public Reports
branch_006.rationale: All low-level goals describe actions by a non-registered user to retrieve, display, and filter public reports using various interfaces and methods. They collectively contribute to the overarching goal of making public reports accessible and viewable to non-registered users.

branch_007.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Provide Public Access to Reporting Statistics
branch_007.rationale: Both low-level goals describe functionalities for non-registered users to view different types of statistics related to reports. One focuses on categorical breakdowns, and the other on temporal trends, but both contribute to the overarching goal of making reporting data publicly accessible for informational purposes.

branch_008.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the essential steps an office staff member undertakes to perform an initial review of reports. This includes identifying reports awaiting review, accessing their full details, and documenting internal observations during the review process.

branch_009.rationale: These operations collectively describe the process by which office staff evaluate citizen reports and make a formal decision regarding their acceptance or rejection, including providing necessary justifications for rejections. They all contribute to the initial handling and disposition of incoming reports.

branch_010.rationale: All low-level goals describe actions related to setting or changing the status of a report at various stages of its lifecycle, from submission to completion or rejection. This ensures proper tracking and workflow management for reports.

branch_011.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the process of identifying approved reports that require assignment, performing the assignment to either internal departments or external personnel/companies, and receiving system support for making these assignments. They all contribute to the overarching goal of effectively directing approved reports to the appropriate parties for further action.

branch_012.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Technical Office Staff to Monitor Report Progress
branch_012.rationale: These operations collectively provide the technical office staff with comprehensive capabilities to view, track, and report on the current status, historical changes, and overall progress of reports and issues assigned to their office. They all contribute to effective oversight and information retrieval regarding report lifecycle management.

branch_013.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the essential steps for technical office staff to track the progress and document the outcome of work performed on a report, from the initiation of active work to its successful completion and the detailed recording of how it was resolved. They all contribute to effectively managing the lifecycle of a report's resolution.

branch_014.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Manage communication with external maintenance personnel regarding assigned reports
branch_014.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the complete lifecycle of communication between technical office staff and external maintenance personnel concerning a specific report: sending messages, receiving responses, and reviewing the entire interaction history. These operations are all integral to effectively managing and tracking communication related to assigned reports.

branch_015.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Manage Assigned Reports for External Maintenance Personnel
branch_015.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the essential steps an external maintenance personnel takes to identify, understand, and formally accept responsibility for reports assigned to them. These operations are all part of the initial phase of managing an assigned report, from discovery to formal acknowledgment.

branch_016.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Facilitate External Maintenance Personnel Reporting of Work Progress and Completion
branch_016.rationale: These low-level goals collectively describe the essential actions for external maintenance personnel to report the lifecycle of their assigned tasks. They cover initiating work, marking it as finished, and providing necessary evidence, all contributing to a comprehensive reporting process for maintenance activities.

branch_017.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable External Maintenance Personnel to Communicate with the Municipal Technical Office regarding Reports
branch_017.rationale: These low-level goals collectively describe the essential functionalities for external maintenance personnel to engage in two-way communication (sending and receiving messages) and maintain an auditable record (viewing history) with the municipal technical office concerning specific reports. They all contribute to establishing and managing this communication channel.

branch_018.rationale: All low-level goals describe various administrative tasks performed by a municipal administrator to set up, customize, and maintain the operational parameters, user access, data structures, and external interfaces of the system. They collectively aim to ensure the system functions according to municipal policies and integrates effectively.

branch_019.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Municipal Administrator to Monitor and Analyze System Performance and Usage
branch_019.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe various methods for the municipal administrator to access, customize, visualize, and export statistical data and reports. These operations are all geared towards providing the administrator with the necessary tools to monitor system performance, understand user interactions, evaluate system health, and conduct in-depth analysis of operational data.

branch_001.rationale: Voting result 3/3 for KEEP_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. The goal 'Submit Urban Issue Reports' is fully supported by the project description (Section A). It represents a distinct, independently satisfiable stakeholder outcome: the creation and submission of a report. While 'Maintain Report Anonymity' is a related capability, it is a specific option/attribute of the submission process rather than a separate end-to-end workflow that subsumes the act of reporting itself. The other citizen goals (Receive Updates, Communicate, Monitor) cover post-submission interactions or different user intents. Therefore, this goal is not redundant and is correctly scoped at the High-Level Goal granularity. Voting result 3/3 for REGENERATE_LOW_LEVEL_GOALS. The current LLGs contain a material defect. 'UploadCitizenProfilePhoto' (llg_003) is unsupported by the documentation for this specific goal; the document mentions uploading a personal photo in the context of user settings (Section C), which is distinct from the core workflow of submitting urban issue reports (Section A). Including it here conflates profile management with report submission. Additionally, the core capability of selecting the anonymity option during the report submission process is missing from the LLGs. Although 'Maintain Report Anonymity' is a sibling HLG, the act of *selecting* this option is an explicit part of the report creation workflow described in Section A ('the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous'). Therefore, the decomposition is incomplete and contains an unsupported element.

While 'Maintain Report Anonymity' is a related capability, it is a specific option/attribute of the submission process rather than a separate end-to-end workflow that subsumes the act of reporting itself. branch_002.rationale: Voting result 2/3 for KEEP_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. The original High-Level Goal 'Receive Report Updates' is supported by the documentation (Section C: CITIZEN UPDATES), which explicitly states that citizens receive notifications at every state change and can receive messages from operators. However, the bottom-up reconstruction 'Enable Citizens to Monitor and Manage Their Submitted Reports' is broader and potentially conflates distinct stakeholder outcomes. The documentation distinguishes between receiving updates/notifications (Section C) and communicating with administration (also Section C, but distinct interaction). More importantly, 'Monitor and Manage' is vague. The specific intent of 'Receive Report Updates' is to stay informed about status changes, which is a distinct outcome from 'Communicate with Administration' (two-way messaging) or 'Monitor Community Issues' (following others). The original goal is appropriately scoped to the notification/update mechanism. The reconstruction is less precise. Therefore, the original goal should be kept as it accurately reflects the documented capability of receiving status updates and notifications. Voting result 3/3 for REGENERATE_LOW_LEVEL_GOALS. The current LLGs contain a material defect. LLG 'llg_004' (ViewReportHistoryLog) is unsupported by the documentation. Section C states that citizens receive notifications at every state change and can view reports on the map/table, but it does not explicitly state that citizens can access a 'chronological log of all updates and actions'. While operators exchange comments, these are explicitly stated to be 'not visible to the reporting citizen'. Therefore, a full history log including actions/comments is not entailed. Additionally, the parent goal 'Receive Report Updates' implies the ability to receive messages from operators (Section C: 'municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message... to which it can reply'). While 'Communicate with Administration' is a sibling HLG, the specific mechanism of receiving these updates/messages is part of the 'Receive Report Updates' flow. However, the most critical error is the unsupported 'History Log'. The LLGs also miss the explicit capability of receiving email notifications (distinct from platform notifications, though linked) and receiving operator messages, which are core parts of 'updates' in Section C. But primarily, llg_004 is an invention not grounded in the text.

branch_003.rationale: Voting result 2/3 for REMOVE_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. The original HLG 'Communicate with Administration' is supported by Section C, which states that 'municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply.' However, this capability is intrinsically linked to the flow of updates described in the sibling HLG 'Receive Report Updates'. Section C groups 'notifications on state change' and 'messages from operators' under the umbrella of 'Citizen Updates' to strengthen trust. The citizen's intention is to stay informed and engaged with the status of their report. Splitting 'receiving status notifications' (Receive Report Updates) from 'exchanging messages' (Communicate with Administration) creates an artificial fragmentation of a single stakeholder outcome: maintaining an information channel with the administration regarding a specific report. The 'Receive Report Updates' goal is the broader, more accurate umbrella for the citizen's interaction with the report's lifecycle information, including both passive notifications and active message exchanges. Therefore, 'Communicate with Administration' is fully redundant with 'Receive Report Updates' in the context of the citizen's end-to-end goal of staying informed. Destructive-action gate: REMOVE was not unanimous; the HLG is retained in this state. Voting result 3/3 for KEEP_LOW_LEVEL_GOALS. The current LLGs accurately decompose the parent HLG 'Communicate with Administration'. Section C explicitly states that 'municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply.' This entails the capabilities to send messages (llg_001), receive messages (llg_002), and view the conversation history (llg_003) to facilitate this exchange. The LLGs are supported by the documentation and do not duplicate the responsibilities of sibling HLGs like 'Receive Report Updates' (which focuses on status change notifications) or 'Monitor Community Issues'. There are no unsupported or missing essential capabilities.

branch_005.rationale: Voting result 3/3 for KEEP_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. The goal 'Monitor Community Issues' is supported by Section C, which states that citizens can 'follow other citizens' open reports and receive notifications'. This is a distinct stakeholder outcome from 'Receive Report Updates' (which focuses on the citizen's *own* reports) and 'Submit Urban Issue Reports'. While viewing public reports is also available to non-registered users (covered by 'Access Public Report Information' for that actor), the ability to *follow* specific reports and receive notifications is a unique capability for registered citizens. Therefore, it is not fully redundant with siblings and represents a valid, independently scoped intention. Voting result 2/3 for REGENERATE_LOW_LEVEL_GOALS. The current LLGs cover browsing and filtering public reports (llg_001, llg_002) and following/unfollowing them (llg_003, llg_004). However, the documentation explicitly states that citizens can view reports on an 'interactive map of Turin' and in a 'summary table'. While llg_001 mentions a 'list', it does not explicitly cover the map view, which is a distinct and essential capability for monitoring community issues as described in Section C. Furthermore, the sibling HLG 'Access Public Report Information' for non-registered users covers viewing the map and table, but the Citizen actor has the specific capability to *follow* reports, which is distinct. The omission of the map view for the Citizen actor is a material defect because the documentation highlights the map as a primary interface for viewing reports. Additionally, 'Monitor Community Issues' implies staying aware, which includes viewing the details of the reports (clicking on the title opens a page with the description), which is not explicitly covered by the current LLGs (browsing list, filtering, following, unfollowing). branch_008.rationale: Voting result 3/3 for REWRITE_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. The original High-Level Goal 'Review Citizen Reports' is supported by Section B, which states that the Organization Office performs a preliminary review of citizen reports. However, the hierarchy for this actor is fragmented. The actor has three HLGs: 'Review Citizen Reports', 'Approve or Reject Reports', and 'Manage Report Workflow'. Section B describes a single end-to-end process where the Organization Office reviews reports and then marks them as accepted or rejected. 'Review' and 'Approve/Reject' are not independently satisfiable stakeholder outcomes; one cannot meaningfully 'review' without the intent to 'approve or reject', and the approval/rejection is the direct outcome of the review. Furthermore, 'Manage Report Workflow' is overly generic and overlaps with the specific actions of reviewing and approving/rejecting for this actor (since the Organization Office only handles the initial state transition). The goal 'Review Citizen Reports' is too narrow as it excludes the decisive action (approval/rejection) which is the primary purpose of the review. Therefore, it should be rewritten to encompass the complete initial processing intention: reviewing and deciding on the validity of reports (approving or rejecting).

replacement_request.generation_project_description:
In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: [https://iris.sad.ve.it/](https://iris.sad.ve.it/?utm_source=gemini). The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source software to all Italian public administrations through the portal [https://developers.italia.it/](https://developers.italia.it/?utm_source=gemini).

A. REPORTS
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin (which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its file path on the server). The possible problem categories are:
• Waterworks – Drinking water
• Architectural Barriers
• Sewerage
• Public Lighting
• Waste
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights
• Roads and Urban Furniture
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds
• Other
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), two cases are possible:

* Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer can mark the report as resolved.
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company (bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if previously configured by the municipal administrator.
* Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state.

C. CITIZEN UPDATES
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo).
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the same rules as for their own reports).

D. STATISTICS
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.

branch_009.rationale: Voting result 3/3 for REWRITE_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. The original High-Level Goal 'Approve or Reject Reports' is supported by the project description (Section B) and the actor definition. However, the hierarchy for 'Organization Office Staff' is fragmented. The actor has three HLGs: 'Review Citizen Reports', 'Approve or Reject Reports', and 'Manage Report Workflow'. Section B describes a single, atomic end-to-end process for this actor: performing a preliminary review and then marking the report as accepted or rejected (with a mandatory explanation for rejection). 'Review' and 'Approve/Reject' are not independently satisfiable stakeholder outcomes; the review is the means to the decision, and the decision is the outcome. 'Manage Report Workflow' is overly generic and overlaps with the specific state transitions performed by this actor (Pending Approval -> Accepted/Rejected). Since no single sibling currently acts as a valid umbrella for the complete initial disposition process, and 'Approve or Reject Reports' captures the decisive outcome of the workflow, it is the best candidate to be rewritten into a broader goal that encompasses the review and the decision. This consolidation will allow the subsequent repair step to generate LLGs for the entire initial processing phase under one coherent intention.

replacement_request.generation_project_description:
In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: [https://iris.sad.ve.it/](https://iris.sad.ve.it/?utm_source=gemini). The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source software to all Italian public administrations through the portal [https://developers.italia.it/](https://developers.italia.it/?utm_source=gemini).

A. REPORTS
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin (which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its file path on the server). The possible problem categories are:
• Waterworks – Drinking water
• Architectural Barriers
• Sewerage
• Public Lighting
• Waste
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights
• Roads and Urban Furniture
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds
• Other
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), two cases are possible:

* Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer can mark the report as resolved.
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company (bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if previously configured by the municipal administrator.
* Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state.

C. CITIZEN UPDATES
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo).
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the same rules as for their own reports).

D. STATISTICS
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.

branch_010.rationale: Voting result 2/3 for REMOVE_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. The sibling goals 'Review Citizen Reports' and 'Approve or Reject Reports' already cover the specific, documented intentions of this actor. 'Manage Report Workflow' does not represent an independently satisfiable stakeholder outcome distinct from these siblings; rather, it is a broad label that overlaps with them but adds no new capability. Since the specific actions are already captured by the siblings, and the generic label implies a scope (full lifecycle management) that this actor does not possess, it is redundant and misleading. However, because 'Review' and 'Approve/Reject' are distinct steps of the same atomic process (initial disposition), they are also fragmented. But for the specific goal 'Manage Report Workflow', it is fully redundant with the combination of the specific siblings or simply an incorrect abstraction. Given the instruction to remove if another HLG covers the intention, and since 'Approve or Reject Reports' is the decisive outcome of the workflow phase this actor controls, 'Manage Report Workflow' is redundant. More precisely, it is a generic container that is not a valid independent goal. It should be removed as it is fully redundant with the specific goals that define the actor's actual work. In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: [https://iris.sad.ve.it/](https://iris.sad.ve.it/?utm_source=gemini). The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source software to all Italian public administrations through the portal [https://developers.italia.it/](https://developers.italia.it/?utm_source=gemini).

A. REPORTS
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin (which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its file path on the server). The possible problem categories are:
• Waterworks – Drinking water
• Architectural Barriers
• Sewerage
• Public Lighting
• Waste
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights
• Roads and Urban Furniture
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds
• Other
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), two cases are possible:

* Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer can mark the report as resolved.
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company (bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if previously configured by the municipal administrator.
* Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state.

C. CITIZEN UPDATES
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo).
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the same rules as for their own reports).

D. STATISTICS
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.

replacement_request.generation_project_description:
In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: [https://iris.sad.ve.it/](https://iris.sad.ve.it/?utm_source=gemini). The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source software to all Italian public administrations through the portal [https://developers.italia.it/](https://developers.italia.it/?utm_source=gemini).

A. REPORTS
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin (which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its file path on the server). The possible problem categories are:
• Waterworks – Drinking water
• Architectural Barriers
• Sewerage
• Public Lighting
• Waste
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights
• Roads and Urban Furniture
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds
• Other
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), two cases are possible:

* Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer can mark the report as resolved.
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company (bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if previously configured by the municipal administrator.
* Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state.

C. CITIZEN UPDATES
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo).
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the same rules as for their own reports).

D. STATISTICS
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.

branch_018.rationale: Voting result 2/3 for KEEP_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. The original High-Level Goal 'Configure System Settings' is supported by the project description, which explicitly mentions that the municipal administrator can configure automatic report assignment rules. However, the bottom-up reconstruction 'Enable System Customization and Administration' better captures the broader scope of the administrator's role, which includes user management and system configuration. The current hierarchy for the Municipal Administrator only includes 'Access Comprehensive Statistics' and 'Configure System Settings'. The description states the administrator is responsible for 'system configuration, user management, and accessing private statistics'. 'Configure System Settings' is a valid but narrow phase of the broader administrative intention. Since 'Access Comprehensive Statistics' covers the statistics aspect, and 'Configure System Settings' covers the configuration aspect, but 'user management' is not explicitly covered by a distinct HLG, the hierarchy is slightly fragmented. However, 'Configure System Settings' is a distinct, independently satisfiable outcome (setting up rules) separate from viewing statistics. It is not redundant. The reconstruction suggests a broader umbrella, but 'Configure System Settings' is precise and supported. Given the specific mention of 'automatic report assignment rules' in the description, this goal is well-scoped. It is not a mere workflow fragment of another goal. It represents a distinct administrative capability. Therefore, it should be kept, as it is supported and independently scoped. The reconstruction is broader but not necessarily more accurate for this specific goal. The original goal is precise. Voting result 3/3 for REGENERATE_LOW_LEVEL_GOALS. The current Low-Level Goals (LLGs) contain several unsupported capabilities. 'DefineReportCategories' (llg_001) is not supported as the description states categories are 'chosen from a predefined list' and does not mention administrator management of this list. 'ManageUserRolesAndPermissions' (llg_003) is unsupported; while the actor description mentions 'user management', the system description only details citizen registration and specific roles for offices/external staff, without detailing an admin interface for role/permission assignment. 'SetNotificationPreferences' (llg_004) is unsupported; the description states citizens can disable email notifications in their *user settings panel*, not that the administrator configures system-wide notification settings. 'EnableChatbotAPIIntegration' (llg_005) is unsupported; the description states the functionality 'must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots', which is a system requirement, not an administrative configuration task. Only 'ConfigureAutomaticAssignmentRules' (llg_002) is explicitly supported by the note in Section B regarding automatic assignment configuration by the municipal administrator. Therefore, the decomposition requires regeneration to remove unsupported LLGs and focus on the documented configuration capabilities.

missing_hlg_evaluation.rationale: Voting result 3/3 for NO_MISSING_HIGH_LEVEL_GOALS. A requirement-by-requirement audit confirms that all explicit functional responsibilities for the identified actors are covered by the current High-Level Goals. Specifically: (1) Citizen capabilities (registration, submission, anonymity, updates, communication, monitoring) are covered by 'Submit Urban Issue Reports', 'Maintain Report Anonymity', 'Receive Report Updates', 'Communicate with Administration', and 'Monitor Community Issues'. (2) Non-Registered User capabilities (viewing public reports and statistics) are covered by 'Access Public Report Information' and 'View Public System Statistics'. (3) Organization Office Staff responsibilities (review, approval/rejection, workflow management) are covered by 'Review Citizen Reports', 'Approve or Reject Reports', and 'Manage Report Workflow'. (4) Technical Office Staff responsibilities (assignment, tracking, status updates, internal communication) are covered by 'Assign Approved Reports', 'Track Report Progress', 'Update Report Status', and 'Facilitate Internal Communication'. (5) External Maintenance Personnel responsibilities (receiving tasks, updating status, communicating) are covered by 'Receive Assigned Tasks', 'Update Work Status', and 'Communicate with Technical Office'. (6) Municipal Administrator responsibilities (configuration, statistics) are covered by 'Configure System Settings' and 'Access Comprehensive Statistics'. No documented actor-level functional requirements remain uncovered.

branch_001.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Citizens to Report Urban Issues
branch_001.rationale: The initial goals (registration, account activation, and profile setup) are foundational steps that establish a citizen's identity and presence within the system. These steps are necessary prerequisites for the subsequent, core functionality of submitting detailed reports about urban issues, which include textual descriptions, multimedia attachments, geographical location, and categorization. All these operations collectively serve the purpose of empowering citizens to effectively communicate and report problems in their urban environment.

branch_002.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Citizens to Monitor and Manage Notifications for Their Submitted Reports
branch_002.rationale: These low-level goals collectively aim to provide citizens with comprehensive capabilities to track the status and history of their submitted reports, as well as to control how they receive real-time updates and notifications regarding those reports. They ensure citizens are informed and have agency over their communication preferences.

branch_003.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the functionalities required for a citizen to engage in a two-way communication with a municipal operator concerning a specific report, including the ability to send messages, receive responses, and review the entire conversation history. This ensures transparency and effective resolution of reports through direct dialogue.

branch_004.rationale: Both low-level goals directly contribute to the overarching objective of allowing citizens to submit reports without their identity being publicly disclosed. One goal focuses on the user's ability to choose this option, and the other focuses on the system's responsibility to enforce it, ensuring the anonymity is maintained.

branch_005.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Citizen monitors public reports submitted by other citizens.
branch_005.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe how a citizen can discover, organize, and stay informed about public reports submitted by other citizens, which are all facets of monitoring these reports.

branch_006.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Non-Registered Users to View and Filter Public Reports
branch_006.rationale: These low-level goals collectively describe various ways a non-registered user can access, display, and refine their view of public reports. They cover different presentation formats (interactive map, summary table) and a filtering mechanism (geographical filter), all contributing to the overarching goal of allowing public access and exploration of these reports.

branch_007.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Provide Public Access to Reporting Statistics
branch_007.rationale: Both low-level goals describe functionalities for non-registered users to view different types of statistics related to reports. One focuses on categorical breakdowns, and the other on temporal trends, but both contribute to the overarching goal of making reporting data publicly accessible for informational purposes.

branch_008.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Manage Citizen Report Evaluation and Status Updates
branch_008.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the complete workflow for Organization Office Staff to review citizen reports. This includes identifying reports awaiting evaluation, accessing their detailed content for informed decision-making, and subsequently updating their status to either 'approved' or 'rejected' based on the evaluation outcome. All operations are integral to the process of evaluating and determining the next steps for citizen reports.

branch_009.rationale: These low-level goals collectively describe the process by which office staff assesses incoming citizen reports to determine their validity and appropriateness. This includes the actions of formally accepting a report, formally declining a report, and providing a mandatory explanation when a report is rejected, all of which are integral steps in the initial validation and screening of citizen submissions.

branch_010.rationale: All low-level goals describe actions related to setting or changing the status of a report at various stages of its lifecycle, from submission to completion or rejection. This ensures proper tracking and workflow management for reports.

branch_011.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the process of identifying approved reports that require assignment, performing the actual assignment to either internal departments or external personnel/companies, and receiving system support for making informed assignment decisions. They all contribute to the overarching objective of ensuring that approved reports are efficiently and correctly directed to the appropriate entities for further action.

branch_012.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Enable Technical Office Staff to Monitor Report Progress
branch_012.rationale: These operations collectively provide the technical office staff with comprehensive capabilities to view, track, and report on the current status, historical changes, and overall progress of reports and issues assigned to their office. They all contribute to effective oversight and information retrieval regarding report lifecycle management.

branch_013.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the actions required by technical office staff to track the progress of a report from the initiation of active work to its successful completion, including documenting the specific details of how it was resolved. These operations are integral to overseeing and completing the resolution of a report.

branch_014.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Manage Communication with External Maintenance Personnel
branch_014.rationale: These operations collectively describe the full lifecycle of communication between technical office staff and external maintenance personnel regarding assigned reports, including sending messages, receiving replies, and reviewing the complete interaction history. Therefore, the overarching goal is to effectively manage this communication.

branch_015.rationale: These operations collectively enable external maintenance personnel to discover, understand, and formally accept responsibility for intervention reports assigned to them, forming the initial phase of their task management workflow.

branch_016.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Facilitate External Maintenance Personnel Reporting of Work Progress and Completion
branch_016.rationale: These low-level goals collectively describe the essential actions for external maintenance personnel to report the lifecycle of their assigned tasks. They cover initiating work, marking it as finished, and providing necessary evidence, all contributing to a comprehensive reporting process for maintenance activities.

branch_017.reconstructed_high_level_goal: Manage communication between external maintenance personnel and the municipal technical office regarding reports
branch_017.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the various facets of communication (sending, receiving, and reviewing history) that external maintenance personnel engage in with the municipal technical office, all specifically pertaining to reports. Therefore, the overarching goal is to manage this communication effectively.

branch_018.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe various administrative and configuration tasks performed by a municipal administrator. These tasks include managing data categories, defining operational rules, controlling user access, setting system-wide behaviors like notifications, and configuring external integrations. All these operations are essential for setting up, customizing, and maintaining the overall functionality and operational parameters of the system.

branch_019.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe various methods for the municipal administrator to access, customize, visualize, and export statistical data and reports. branch_001.rationale: Voting result 3/3 for KEEP_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. The original High-Level Goal 'Submit Urban Issue Reports' is fully supported by the project description, which details the citizen's ability to select a location, fill out a form with mandatory fields (title, description, category), attach photos, and choose anonymity. This represents a distinct, independently satisfiable stakeholder outcome (reporting a problem) that is separate from other citizen goals like receiving updates, communicating, or monitoring community issues. The bottom-up reconstruction 'Enable Citizens to Report Urban Issues' is semantically equivalent to the original but slightly more generic. The original name is precise and accurately reflects the specific action and artifact involved. There is no redundancy with sibling goals, as 'Maintain Report Anonymity' is a specific option within the submission process, not a separate end-to-end workflow, and 'Monitor Community Issues' refers to viewing others' reports. Therefore, the original goal should be kept. Voting result 3/3 for REGENERATE_LOW_LEVEL_GOALS. The current LLGs contain a material defect. LLG 'llg_003' (UploadCitizenProfilePhoto) is unsupported by the documentation for this specific goal. The project description states that users can upload a personal photo in the 'user settings panel' (Section C), which is a profile management feature, not a prerequisite or component of the 'Submit Urban Issue Reports' workflow. Including it here conflates profile management with report submission. Additionally, the decomposition is incomplete as it omits the explicit step of selecting the anonymity option, which is a mandatory part of the submission process described in Section A ('the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous'). While registration (llg_001, llg_002) is a prerequisite, it is often modeled separately, but given the prompt's focus on the submission goal, the inclusion of profile photo upload is clearly out of scope for this specific HLG, and the missing anonymity selection is a key part of the submission form logic.

replacement_request.generation_project_description:
In the Municipality of Turin, a system called Participium is being developed — an information system that enables citizen participation in the management of urban environments. It allows citizens to interact with the public administration by reporting inconveniences and malfunctions found in the city (e.g., potholes in the asphalt, sidewalks with architectural barriers, garbage in the streets, broken streetlights, etc.). An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: [https://iris.sad.ve.it/](https://iris.sad.ve.it/?utm_source=gemini). The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source software to all Italian public administrations through the portal [https://developers.italia.it/](https://developers.italia.it/?utm_source=gemini).

A. REPORTS
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin (which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its file path on the server). The possible problem categories are:
• Waterworks – Drinking water
• Architectural Barriers
• Sewerage
• Public Lighting
• Waste
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights
• Roads and Urban Furniture
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds
• Other
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue resolution has started. An example of a similar information system is IRIS in Venice: [https://iris.sad.ve.it/](https://iris.sad.ve.it/?utm_source=gemini). The system, once developed, will be made available as open-source software to all Italian public administrations through the portal [https://developers.italia.it/](https://developers.italia.it/?utm_source=gemini).

A. REPORTS
Citizens can submit reports only if they have registered in the system with a username, first name, and last name. Once the registration is received, the user gets an email with a confirmation link. The registration becomes valid, and the user can use the system only after confirming through that link. Once registered, a citizen can submit reports by selecting a point on the map of Turin (which will be saved with latitude and longitude values) and filling in a problem form with the following mandatory fields: title, textual description, category (chosen from a predefined list). It is also mandatory to attach one or more photos (up to 3 per report, with each photo stored with its file path on the server). The possible problem categories are:
• Waterworks – Drinking water
• Architectural Barriers
• Sewerage
• Public Lighting
• Waste
• Road Signs and Traffic Lights
• Roads and Urban Furniture
• Public Green Areas and Playgrounds
• Other
After entering all the information and the pictures, the system asks the citizen whether they want the report to be anonymous (the name will not appear in the public list of all reports).

B. REPORT LIFECYCLE
Once submitted, the report is in the “Pending Approval” state until the Organization Office of the Municipality of Turin performs a preliminary review of citizen reports, marking them as accepted or rejected. The possible states for a report are: Pending Approval, In Progress, Work in Progress, Suspended, Rejected. After approval, accepted reports move to the “In Progress” state, at which point they are assigned to the technical office responsible, based on the problem category. Once the intervention is planned, the state changes to “Work in Progress”, indicating that the issue resolution has started. In some cases, for organizational or technical reasons, the report can be set to “Suspended”, awaiting further evaluation or resources. When the problem is solved, the technical office updates the status and closes the report. In case of rejection, a written explanation from the Organization Office is mandatory (see next section).
If the intervention must be carried out by maintenance personnel from an external company (for example, Enel X for Public Lighting, or company Y for specific reports based on their content), two cases are possible:

* Case 1: The company has access to Participium. In this case, the technical office assigns the report to users from the corresponding company. External maintenance personnel can move the report from Assigned to In Progress. Staff from the technical office and external maintenance workers can exchange information and comments through the report, but these are not visible to the reporting citizen (nor to other citizens). Once the work is completed, the external maintainer can mark the report as resolved.
Note: Automatic assignment of all reports in a certain category to the external company (bypassing the initial review by the public relations officer of the municipality) is possible only if previously configured by the municipal administrator.
* Case 2: The company does NOT have access to Participium. In this case, the external company updates the technical office outside Participium, and once the problems are solved, a staff member from the technical office will manually move the report to the Resolved state.

C. CITIZEN UPDATES
To strengthen trust between citizens and institutions, the citizen can receive updates regarding their own reports through various channels. First, at every state change, the citizen receives a notification on the platform with the corresponding update. Furthermore, municipal operators updating reports can send the reporting citizen a message through the platform, to which it can reply. The system must allow this functionality to be accessible by external chatbots as well. Each time the citizen receives a notification on the platform, they also get an email (this option can be disabled in the user settings panel, where they can also upload a personal photo).
Moreover, after the approval phase, accepted reports immediately become visible on the Participium portal: they appear both on an interactive map of Turin, geolocated based on the citizen’s selected point, and in a summary table that allows filtering and sorting reports by category, status, or date. In both views, the reporter’s name (“anonymous” if that option was chosen) and the report title are displayed. Clicking on the title opens a page with the description.
Even non-registered users can view both the maps and the summary table. Once logged into Participium, citizens can follow other citizens’ open reports and receive notifications (following the same rules as for their own reports).

D. STATISTICS
The system allows viewing public and private statistics. Public statistics are visible in a dedicated section of the website and concern the number of reports per category, and trends over day, week, or month. They are also visible to non-registered users. In the private section, accessible only to administrators, it is possible to view, in addition to the public statistics, charts and tables.

branch_016.rationale: Voting result 3/3 for REWRITE_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. The original High-Level Goal 'Update Work Status' is a specific workflow phase (state transition) rather than an independent stakeholder outcome. The actor description explicitly states that External Maintenance Personnel 'are assigned specific reports to resolve and update their status within the system.' The current hierarchy fragments this single end-to-end intention into three separate HLGs: 'Receive Assigned Tasks', 'Update Work Status', and 'Communicate with Technical Office'. These capabilities are tightly coupled and operate on the same artifact (the assigned report) to achieve the single outcome of resolving the issue. 'Update Work Status' is not independently satisfiable as a stakeholder goal; it is the core action of the broader task management process. Therefore, the hierarchy is fragmented. The broadest suitable goal, 'Update Work Status', should be rewritten to serve as the umbrella for the entire post-assignment management lifecycle, encompassing receiving/accessing the task, updating status, and communicating with the technical office to ensure resolution.

branch_018.rationale: Voting result 3/3 for REWRITE_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. The original High-Level Goal 'Configure System Settings' is supported by the project description, which explicitly mentions that the municipal administrator configures system settings, including automatic report assignment rules. However, the actor description also explicitly lists 'user management' as a core responsibility. The current hierarchy for the Municipal Administrator only contains 'Access Comprehensive Statistics' and 'Configure System Settings'. The goal 'Configure System Settings' is too narrow as it does not encompass the 'user management' aspect of the administrator's role, which is a distinct and documented stakeholder intention. The bottom-up reconstruction 'Manage System Configuration and Administration' better captures the full scope of the administrator's administrative duties, including both configuration and user management. Therefore, the goal should be rewritten to reflect this broader, more accurate scope.

branch_019.rationale: Voting result 2/3 for KEEP_ORIGINAL_HIGH_LEVEL_GOAL. The original High-Level Goal 'Access Comprehensive Statistics' is supported by the project description, which explicitly states that administrators can view private statistics including charts and tables. However, the actor description defines the Municipal Administrator's responsibilities as 'system configuration, user management, and accessing private statistics.' The current hierarchy for this actor contains 'Configure System Settings' and 'Access Comprehensive Statistics', but lacks a goal for 'User Management'. While 'Access Comprehensive Statistics' is a valid and distinct stakeholder outcome (analysis/oversight) separate from configuration, the bottom-up reconstruction 'Monitor and Analyze System Performance and Usage' is semantically equivalent and arguably more precise regarding the intent (analysis vs. mere access). More importantly, the hierarchy is fragmented: the administrator's role is split into configuration and statistics, missing user management. However, the specific goal 'Access Comprehensive Statistics' is not redundant with 'Configure System Settings' (different artifacts/intents: data vs. config). It is a valid, independently satisfiable outcome. The reconstruction suggests a slight refinement in wording ('Monitor and Analyze' vs 'Access'), but 'Access' is also acceptable. Given the rubric, the goal is supported and independently scoped. The missing 'User Management' is a hierarchy omission but does not invalidate this specific HLG. missing_hlg_evaluation.rationale: Voting result 3/3 for NO_MISSING_HIGH_LEVEL_GOALS. The project description's functional requirements are fully covered by the current High-Level Goals. Section A (Reports) is covered by 'Submit Urban Issue Reports' and 'Maintain Report Anonymity'. Section B (Lifecycle) is covered by 'Manage Initial Citizen Report Processing' (which entails the review outcome of the retired 'Review Citizen Reports'), 'Approve or Reject Reports', 'Manage Report Workflow', 'Assign Approved Reports', 'Track Report Progress', 'Update Report Status', and 'Facilitate Internal Communication'. Section C (Updates) is covered by 'Receive Report Updates', 'Communicate with Administration', 'Monitor Community Issues', and 'Access Public Report Information'. Section D (Statistics) is covered by 'View Public System Statistics' and 'Access Comprehensive Statistics'. The retired goal 'Review Citizen Reports' is semantically entailed by 'Manage Initial Citizen Report Processing', which explicitly includes evaluating and determining validity. No explicit actor-level functional requirements are left uncovered.

branch_001.rationale: The initial goals (llg_001, llg_002, llg_003) focus on establishing and personalizing a citizen's account, which is a prerequisite for participating in the system. The subsequent goals (llg_004, llg_005, llg_006, llg_007) detail the process of submitting comprehensive reports about urban issues. Together, these operations form a complete flow for citizens to engage with a platform designed for reporting community problems.

branch_002.rationale: The low-level goals collectively aim to provide citizens with comprehensive tools to track the status and history of their submitted reports, receive timely updates, and control their notification preferences. This ensures citizens are well-informed and have agency over their interactions with the reporting system.

branch_003.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the functionalities required for a citizen to engage in a two-way communication with a municipal operator concerning a specific report, including the ability to send messages, receive responses, and review the entire conversation history. This ensures transparency and effective resolution of reports through direct dialogue.

branch_004.rationale: Both low-level goals directly contribute to the overarching objective of allowing citizens to submit reports without their identity being publicly disclosed. One goal focuses on the user's ability to choose this option, and the other focuses on the system's responsibility to enforce it, ensuring the anonymity is maintained.
